title: Seva of the hands
hookLine: washing dishes, sweeping, cooking: the body's seva
last: JODA GHAR — START AT THE SHOES.

cards: The back of a big gurdwara kitchen, after langar. A mountain of steel plates, the kind with little sections for dal and rice and sweet. Along a trough of hot, soapy water stands a line of people.
One scrapes. One scrubs. One rinses.
One dries and stacks. Their sleeves are soaked. Nobody is in charge of anyone.

A teenager is next to a man who runs a company, and they've fallen into the same rhythm, plate after plate. It looks like the chore you get through before the spiritual part. Sikhs would say this is the spiritual part.

teach.h: TAN, MAN, DHAN: BODY, MIND, WEALTH.
teach.b: Sikhs often talk about seva in three ways: tan, man and dhan. Body, mind and wealth. Today is tan, the body's seva: washing, sweeping, cooking, carrying, fixing.
Tomorrow, the purse. After that, the mind. Why does the body's seva matter so much?

teach.h: KIND THOUGHTS ARE EASY; POTS AREN'T.
teach.b: Kind thoughts are easy. Scrubbing someone else's pot is harder, and pride feels it. When your hands do the humble work, the teaching goes all the way in.
You met the model on day forty-nine.

Before he became the third Guru, Amar Das was an old man who carried water for Guru Angad, before dawn, from the river, for years. Tradition says he never let the work stop, even in the dark and the rain.

The Guru he became was shaped by those buckets. Among the saloks of Kabir in the Guru Granth Sahib, Namdev tells Trilochan, in paraphrase: do all your work with hands and feet, and keep your mind with the Pure One.

teach.h: HANDS AT WORK, HEART WITH THE BELOVED.
teach.b: Punjabis put it shorter: hands at work, heart with the beloved. You don't have to choose between doing and remembering.
While the hands wash, the mind can say Waheguru. While the broom moves, the heart can be still. The chore becomes a kind of prayer.

Hands teach one more thing: work done together makes a sangat. It's hard to stay angry with someone after an hour side by side, passing them wet plates. So in Sikh life the hands aren't the servants of the spirit.
They're one of the ways the spirit gets anywhere at all.

how: In gurdwaras, Sikhs and visitors volunteer to cook, clean, sweep and wash the langar dishes, often reciting or listening to gurbani as they work.

o: the bowing and sitting postures used during prayer
service done with the body: washing, sweeping, cooking
a fast that disciplines the body before morning worship

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: washing dishes is the chore before the spiritual part

the third Guru served by carrying water before he became Guru

games.q: you're washing plates after langar, and your mind wanders to your to-do list. what does today's couplet suggest?
o: hurry, so you can get to the real prayer.
hands at work, heart with the beloved.
stop washing until your mind is quiet.
games.why: you don't have to choose: the hands can work while the heart remembers. the chore becomes a kind of prayer.

practice: Wash one dish slowly, a cup, a plate, even a spoon, feeling the water's warmth and turning it in your hands; if you can't get to a sink, wipe any object near you clean with the same care.
With each movement, let a word ride along: Waheguru, if you like, or just thank you.

wordCard.voice: Tan seva. The body's service: washing, sweeping, cooking, carrying, done with the heart somewhere else, somewhere good.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: body, mind, wealth, the three ways of seva.

carryVoice: Your line: hands can pray. The dishes count too. See you tomorrow.
